Windows 10 piggy backs your bandwidth to distribute patches

Delivery Optimization downloads the same updates and apps that you get through Windows Update and the Windows Store. Delivery Optimization creates a local cache, and stores files that it has downloaded in that cache for a short period of time. Depending on your settings, Windows then send parts of those files to other PCs on your local network or PCs on the Internet that are downloading the same files.

Technically you are like a seeder from a torrent site. It does not say how much data using up your hard disk space, it also does not state how much is sent to other users?

It also does not state if Windows 8.1 users are now transmitting Windows 10 to the rest of the world?

It might very well have been transmitting 100s of Windows 10 copies to the world using your bandwidth. I think it is time to investigate deeper how that technology works.
Yeah, it just strikes me as something that seemed like a good idea when someone at Microsoft came up with it, but the implications and bandwidth usage wasn't thought through.
Or you could ask people who have it installed if their bandwidth usage has changed?

If they took the same attitude with the desktop they would look very good compared to the Googles and Apples.

Final Fantasy: Crystal Chronicles (the original, not FF:CC:Ring of Fates or Echoes of Time "sequels" which just weren't fun at all)...

Problem: Multiplayer required major additional hardware (one GBA + one link cable per player).

Multiplayer was insanely fun though. While you all had a collective goal (beat the level) and cooperation was required/beneficial (e.g. someone had to move/carry the chalice, and simultaneously casting magic at the same target boosted/changed the effect like Fire + Fire = Fira or Firaga depending on how perfectly you timed it) each player had an individual goal (e.g. defeat enemies with melee, or eat food, or collect money). At the end of the level the game ranked you based on how well you completed your individual goals which determined who got first pick of the loot.

So while you had to work together, you simultaneously (and secretly) had to work selfishly. Even the most altruistic actions were suspect: "Why are you healing me so much?" or "Why are you so willing to carry the chalice?"

It was a combination that was done pefectly, that I loved, and have not seen repeated. Yet it was so hard to get a good multiplayer session going because of the hardware requirements.
